answer.rationale: The binding constraint is that primary supply lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew while the line runs at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. Any option that does not secure primary supply this cycle (add_second_source, defer_decision) leaves an uncovered gap, and defer_decision only worked in memory_c5 for a non-critical, month-to-month service, which does not transfer here. negotiate_terms (memory_c4) is directly blocked: the incumbent has already refused to reopen price this cycle, so the lever that recovered margin before is unavailable. switch_primary_vendor is the only single move that plausibly reaches the full 18% on unit cost, but memory_c2 is a single favorable prior year and says nothing about migrating under a 14-day cliff at 94% utilization with zero buffer; onboarding that was 'quick' under slack conditions is not evidence it is safe under none. That leaves renewal as the risk-controlled base (memory_c1: stable integration, no migration, no interruption), structured with the memory_c6 lever - a longer term commitment unlocking volume pricing without narrowing service scope - because term length is a distinct lever from reopening this cycle's price and may be available even after the price refusal. I want the archive on memory_c2 to see whether the cost win came with scope, volume, or timing conditions that would not hold here, and on memory_c6 to see the actual discount magnitude and lock-in duration, since if the volume tier gets nowhere near 18% the honest conclusion is that renewal is a delivery-risk decision that does not meet the finance mandate. Explicit downstream risk: this choice likely underdelivers on the 18% cut, so the residual gap must be logged as an open obligation for the next review rather than treated as solved, and a multi-year lock could foreclose the switch option later precisely when the cost pressure is still unresolved. I am not treating the inherited records as settled proof - each describes one favorable outcome under conditions that may not match a no-buffer, hard-deadline cycle.
